Stated Claim / Post Context:
Jasmine Crockett Snubs Talarico, Revealing Former Opponent’s Weakness With Black Voters

‘There’s no pulse’

Actual Article Body:
(Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Democratic Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett released her down-ballot endorsements in key state races but notably left out the most crucial candidate on the ticket.

Crockett refrained from endorsing her former opponent, Democratic Senate nominee Texas state Rep. James Talarico, on Monday, highlighting his continued struggle to court black voters. Although a majority of black voters supported Crockett in the primary, Talarico defeated the Democratic congresswoman in March with 53 percent while Crockett lagged behind at 45 percent. (RELATED: Dems Worry James Talarico Lacks Support From Black Voters To Win Texas Senate Race)

“These endorsements reflect candidates who have committed to showing up and fighting for their voters,” Crockett said in a statement. “Candidates who will get to work immediately to lower their prices, stop the attacks on our civil rights, and deliver results.”

“These aren’t the candidates that end up on national TV to make headlines, but they are the ones who make decisions about our healthcare, housing, and economy,” Crockett added. “These are the races that will make a difference in your neighborhood and the seats we have to win.”

Talarico’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment from the Daily Caller.

Talarico’s campaign has been grappling with low enthusiasm among black voters.

The demographic overwhelmingly favored Talarico’s opponent, but he has struggled to maintain their support. One Texas Southern University poll put Talarico at 79 percent favorability with black voters. Another poll from the Texas Politics Project put Talarico at just 67 percent favorability. (RELATED: Jasmine Crockett Honors Convicted Woman Beater Chris Brown At Concert)

Prior Democratic Texas Senate nominees like Colin Allred and Beto O’Rourke won 84 percent and 90 percent of the black vote in their respective general elections.

A black community organizer named Durrell Douglas asked other black residents in Houston, Texas, what they thought about Talarico, giving the New York Times a very candid anecdote.

“There’s no pulse,” Douglas told the Times. “No energy.”
